Hero.subtitle: Build hypnotic bouncing-ball simulations in your browser: tune the physics, stack rainbow effects, pick one of 12 modes and export a vertical MP4 that is ready to post. Free, no account, nothing to install.
Hero.mobileNotice: For the best experience, use a desktop or laptop browser. Controls are optimised for larger screens.

SimulatorPage.metaTitle: Ball Physics Simulator – Free Online Tool for TikTok & Reels – {siteName}
SimulatorPage.metaDescription: Free browser-based ball physics simulator with 12 modes, customisable physics, rainbow effects and MP4 export in vertical TikTok format. No sign-up, no install.

Layout.metaTitle: Free Satisfying Ball Physics Simulator for TikTok & Reels – {siteName}
Layout.metaDescription: Free browser-based ball physics simulator. Create mesmerising bouncing-ball simulations with customisable physics, rainbow effects and 12 unique modes, then export MP4 videos for TikTok, Reels and Shorts. No sign-up or installation needed.
Layout.browserRequirements: Requires a modern web browser with JavaScript enabled
features: MP4 video export in multiple resolutions

Simulator.doNotChangeSettingsWarning: ⚠️ Please do not change settings during playback to ensure simulation accuracy.
Simulator.canvasPendulumInLine: All [count] pendulums back in phase after [cycles] cycle(s)
Simulator.finderEndless: This run never ends with the current settings (an endless mode, Rain, the countdown off or the cycles set to never), so there is no duration to search for.
Simulator.finderFixed: A Pendulum Wave always lasts exactly {duration}s with these settings (the cycles × the cycle length), whatever the seed. Change the cycle length or the number of cycles in the Pendulum wave block to hit the target.
Simulator.recordingUnsupported: Video recording is not supported in this browser. Try a recent version of Chrome, Edge or Firefox.
Simulator.exportFormatNote: Exports as MP4 where the browser supports it, otherwise WebM.
Simulator.canvasPolyrhythmAligned: All [count] voices back in phase after [cycles] cycle(s)
Simulator.finderFixedPolyrhythm: Metronomes & Polyrhythms always lasts exactly {duration}s with these settings (the cycles × the cycle length), whatever the seed. Change the cycle length, the tempos or the number of cycles in the Mode row to hit the target.
Simulator.finderMpTestedClosest: Tested {tested} seeds. The closest final count was {closest} (target: {target} ±5 %)

step1.title: Pick a Mode
step1.description: Choose one of 12 simulation modes: classic rings, paint trails, shatter, colour match, grow, ball drop and more.

step2.title: Customise Everything
step2.description: Adjust physics, colours, effects, text overlays and the look of the ball until the clip feels like yours.

step3.title: Export & Share
step3.description: Record the run as an MP4 in any resolution, including vertical TikTok format, and post it wherever you like.

Controls.accumulationEscapeTip: Seconds the ball has to escape before it freezes in place.
Controls.spikesTip: Add inward-pointing spikes on the outer wall as obstacles.
Controls.spikeCountTip: Number of spikes evenly distributed around the outer wall.
Controls.spawnCountTip: How many new balls spawn each time one escapes a wall.
Controls.targetCountTip: How many numbered segments to place on the wall.
Controls.randomOrderTip: Shuffle the position of target numbers around the wall.
Controls.colorCountTip: How many distinct colours are used on the wall segments. Fewer colours = easier to match.
Controls.ballSpeedTip: How fast the ball moves. Higher values make the simulation more energetic.
Controls.ballSizeTip: Radius of the ball in pixels. Larger balls have a harder time fitting through gaps.
Controls.gravityTip: Downward pull on the ball. Set to 0 for zero-gravity floating.
Controls.twoBallsTip: Spawn a second ball moving in the opposite direction for double the action.
Controls.bouncierTip: Ball gets faster with every wall bounce, building momentum until it escapes.
Controls.ballInteractionTip: What balls do to each other: bounce off (the default), merge into one bigger ball when they touch, split in two every time a ball breaks through a wall, or pass straight through each other. Deterministic: shared links, presets and Find Simulation include it.
Controls.interactionMergeDesc: Touching balls fuse into one ball with their combined area and momentum and a blended colour.
Controls.interactionSplitDesc: Every wall break splits the ball into two halves of half the area that fly apart – down to the smallest size and up to the ball cap.
Controls.interactionPassDesc: Balls ignore each other and fly straight through.
Controls.splitMinRadiusTip: A ball only splits while both halves would still be at least this big.
Controls.maxBallsTip: Splitting stops once this many balls are in play.
Controls.advancedPhysicsTip: Extra forces and wall behaviours. All of them are off by default, so a shared link or a found seed behaves exactly as before until you change them.
Controls.advancedPhysicsDesc: Deterministic extras: shared links, presets and Find Simulation include them.
Controls.airDragTip: Fraction of the ball's speed lost on every physics step (60 per second). A little makes the ball settle; a lot makes it sink.
Controls.windXTip: Constant sideways push, as a fraction of the ball speed gained every second. Negative blows left, positive right.
Controls.windYTip: Constant vertical push. Negative lifts the ball, positive presses it down.
Controls.spinStrengthTip: Wall contact makes the ball spin (rotating walls add their own twist) and the spin curves its flight like a Magnus effect. Custom ball images and emoji rotate with it.
Controls.rotatingGravityTip: Turns the direction of gravity by this many degrees per second, so "down" slowly circles around the arena.
Controls.wallBouncinessTip: How much speed the ball keeps when it rebounds off a wall. Below 100% every hit slows it down; above 100% every hit adds a kick.
Controls.breathingWallsTip: Walls grow and shrink around their normal size by this much; the gaps move with them.
Controls.breathingSpeedTip: How many pulses per second the walls breathe.
Controls.wallCountTip: Number of concentric circular walls the ball must break through.
Controls.wallThicknessTip: Thickness of each wall ring in pixels.
Controls.gapSizeTip: Size of the opening in each wall. Larger gaps make it easier for the ball to escape.
Controls.rotationTip: Walls rotate over time, making the gaps move around the circle.
Controls.trailsTip: Show a fading trail behind the ball as it moves.
Controls.ballGlowTip: Radial light effect around the ball.
Controls.wallGlowTip: Walls flash with colour when the ball bounces off them.
Controls.colorTrailTip: Rainbow hue-shifting trail behind the ball.
Controls.reactiveBgTip: Background pulses and shifts colour on each bounce.
Controls.cameraFollowTip: Smoothly shifts the viewport to keep the ball centred.
Controls.cinematicTip: Subtly steers rebounds to create near-misses and dramatic escapes. Turn off for pure physics.
Controls.trailThicknessTip: How thick the ball's trail is. Higher values create a bolder streak.
Controls.wallBreakEffectTip: Visual effect that plays when the ball breaks through a wall.
Controls.wallBreakSoundDesc: Play a custom audio clip instead of the default tones when the ball breaks through a wall.
Controls.hitSoundModeTip: What plays when the ball bounces off a wall: the synthesised tones (or a melody) or an audio clip of your own.
Controls.hitSampleDesc: Pick a built-in clip or upload your own. It plays on every wall bounce and is included in recordings.
Controls.hitSamplePitchByWallTip: Inner walls play the clip at a higher pitch and outer walls lower, following the same curve as the default tones.
Controls.hitSampleVolumeTip: Loudness of the hit sample relative to the other sounds.
Controls.hitSampleDecodeError: Could not decode this audio file – the synth tones play instead. Try an MP3, OGG, WAV or M4A file.
Controls.customSoundDesc: Choose a song to use its melody as bounce sounds. Each wall hit plays the next note from the song.
Controls.midiSourceText: Not sure where to get MIDI files? Try
Controls.midiParseError: Failed to parse MIDI file. Make sure it is a valid format 0 or 1 MIDI file.
Controls.sliceSongTip: The viral format: upload any song and every bounce plays the next little piece of it, so the ball "plays" the track.
Controls.sliceSongDesc: Upload an MP3, OGG, WAV or M4A file. Each wall hit plays the next slice of the song, continuing from where the last one stopped. The song stays in your browser.
Controls.sliceEnabledTip: While on, slices of the uploaded song replace the bounce tones and melody notes.
Controls.sliceLengthTip: How much of the song each bounce plays. Short slices sound choppy and rhythmic; long ones let whole phrases through.
Controls.sliceLoopTip: Start the song over when it reaches the end. When off, bounces go back to the default tones after the last slice.
Controls.sliceFadeTip: Fade-in and fade-out at the edges of every slice so the cuts don't click.
Controls.sliceDecodeError: Could not decode this audio file. Try an MP3, OGG, WAV or M4A file.
Controls.sliceNoSong: Upload a song to hear it – the default tones play until then.
Controls.musicBedTip: Mixes a music track under the bounce sounds and records it into the exported video, so the clip is ready to post. The file stays in your browser.
Controls.musicBedDesc: Upload an MP3, OGG, WAV or M4A file to play under the bounce sounds. It dips on every hit so the tones stay clear, then swells back. The track stays in your browser.
Controls.musicDecodeError: Could not decode this audio file. Try an MP3, OGG, WAV or M4A file.
Controls.musicVolumeTip: How loud the music plays under the bounce sounds – in the speakers and in the exported video.
Controls.musicDuckingTip: How much the music dips on every bounce and wall break. 0% keeps it steady, 100% mutes it for an instant, like a sidechain compressor.
Controls.musicDuckReleaseTip: How long the music takes to swell back after a bounce, in milliseconds. Short is punchy, long is smooth.
Controls.musicLoopTip: Start the track again when it ends. Off: the music stops at the end of the track and stays silent until the next run.
Controls.musicStartOffsetTip: Skip the first seconds of the track so the drop lands right when the simulation starts. Restarts begin from here too.
Controls.instrumentDesc: The voice the wall tones are played with (a melody picks its own instrument below). Pluck, marimba and chip are synthesised live; the classic tone is Triangle.
Controls.melodyInstrumentDesc: The voice the notes of the chosen song are played with. Sine is the classic melody sound.
Controls.scaleDesc: Snap wall tones and melody notes to the nearest note of a scale so every bounce is in key. Chromatic keeps the original pitches.
Controls.beatLockTip: Delays each bounce sound to the next point of the beat grid (at most one grid step) so exports sit on the beat.
Controls.beatLockDesc: Play bounce sounds on a BPM grid; extra hits inside the same step are skipped so the rhythm stays clean.
Controls.durationTip: The simulation will automatically stop and save after this many seconds.
Controls.watermarkTip: Text displayed faintly in the centre of your exported recording.
Controls.saveHint: Save your current setup (colours, physics, effects) to use later.
Controls.growthRateTip: How fast the ball grows with each bounce (as a percentage).
Controls.centerDotTip: Place a small dot in the centre of the circle that the ball bounces off.
Controls.growLinesTip: Draw lines from each bounce point to the ball, like in Lines mode.
Controls.dropDesc: Balls of different sizes and weights rain through rows of pegs and bars. Every hit plays a note pitched by the ball's size, so the run composes its own polyrhythm.
Controls.dropBallCountTip: How many balls are released from the top of the board.
Controls.dropSizeVariationTip: How far the ball sizes spread around the Ball Size setting. Bigger balls play lower notes.
Controls.dropGravityVariationTip: Gives every ball its own gravity, from floaty to heavy, so they fall out of step and the rhythm keeps shifting.
Controls.dropRowsTip: Number of staggered rows of pegs and bars between the top and the floor.
Controls.dropSpawnIntervalTip: Seconds between two balls leaving the top. 0 drops them all at once.
Controls.dropLoopTip: Opens the floor: balls that fall out of the bottom come back in at the top, so the piece never ends.
Controls.picturePaintTip: Upload any picture and the ball reveals it stroke by stroke – in rhythm with your song, steered so the whole picture appears, paced to finish when the song ends.
Controls.picturePaintDesc: PNG, JPG, WebP or GIF (first frame). The picture is fitted into the circle and stays in your browser; the ball's brush uncovers it and the run ends at 95 % revealed.
Controls.paintPictureError: Could not load this picture. Try a PNG, JPG, WebP or GIF file.
Controls.paintGhostTip: How visible the unrevealed part of the picture is, as a dim greyscale ghost, so viewers can guess what is coming.
Controls.paintBrushTip: Radius of each brush dab as a multiple of the ball. Pace to Song still resizes it to finish on time.
Controls.paintBeatSyncTip: The ball speeds up on every beat and glides in between; the brush and the glow pulse with it. Deterministic, so a recording replays exactly.
Controls.paintBeatSyncDesc: Moves the ball in rhythm: a kick on each beat, a glide until the next. Needs a song with a detectable beat or the manual BPM.
Controls.paintNoSong: Upload a song (Background Music or Song Slicer in the Custom Sound section) to detect its beat, or use the manual BPM.
Controls.paintNoBeat: No steady beat found in this song – use the manual BPM.
Controls.paintBeatPulseTip: How hard each beat kicks the ball: 0 % glides evenly, 100 % doubles the speed on the beat.
Controls.paintGuidedTip: Turns every rebound a little (up to 18°) toward the largest unrevealed area, so the whole picture appears instead of one corner.
Controls.paintGuidedDesc: Meticulous: rebounds aim at what is still hidden.
Controls.paintPaceTip: Resizes the brush every second so the reveal finishes when the song – or the clip – ends. The HUD shows whether the ball is on schedule.
Controls.paintPaceDesc: Finish the reveal with the song (or with the clip length without one).
Controls.dropLoopDesc: Off: the run ends once every ball has come to rest on the floor.
Controls.boxDesc: A box instead of rings. Squares, circles or DVD-style logos fly in straight lines and every wall hit plays a note: the next note of the melody, or one of four notes per wall without one. The numbers count down per bounce, colours cycle and the shapes grow a little.
Controls.boxShapeTip: What bounces around the box: axis-aligned squares, circles or a rounded DVD-style logo whose corner hits are accented with a louder note and a flash.
Controls.boxShapeCountTip: How many shapes start from the centre of the box. They pass through each other, so their rhythms never disturb one another.
Controls.boxSpeedRatioTip: Speeds of the shapes in small whole-number ratios: with 2:3 the second shape hits the walls three times while the first hits twice – that is the polyrhythm. With 1:1 every shape gets its own launch angle instead. The fastest shape moves at the Ball Speed times the seed's tempo (±15 %), which is what lets Find Simulation hit an exact clip length.
Controls.boxSpeedRatioDesc: The launch angle is chosen so each shape's top/bottom and left/right hits form a small ratio of their own. A DVD logo always gets an odd ratio and is re-aimed by a hair at every bounce, so it reaches a corner exactly every 3–13 hits – even while it grows.
Controls.boxCountdownTip: The number on every shape counts down by one per wall hit and the run ends when every shape reaches zero. 0 switches the countdown off and the shapes bounce forever.
Controls.boxGrowPerHitTip: How much a shape grows with every wall hit, as a percentage of its size (capped so it never fills the box).
Controls.boxGravityTip: How much of the Gravity setting acts on the shapes. 0 is the classic straight-line DVD motion; anything above turns the shapes into bouncing balls that keep their bounce height.
Controls.boxAspectTip: Width of the box relative to its height: 9:16 fills a vertical clip, 1:1 is a square, 16:9 is landscape.
Controls.pwDesc: Pendulums tuned like the classic pendulum wave: the slowest swings K times per cycle and each next one once more, so the row drifts into travelling waves, splits into groups and snaps back in line at the end of every cycle. Every centre crossing plays a note pitched by the pendulum's place in the row.
Controls.pwLayoutTip: Where the pendulums hang: a row under a bar (strings visibly different in length), an arc of pivots swinging toward the centre, bobs moving along radii from the centre (optionally on a rotating polygon), the same on a slowly turning frame that draws spiral arms, bobs sliding on rails, or balls bouncing on a floor with periods in the same series.
Controls.pwPolygonTip: Maps the bobs of the Circle and Galaxy layouts onto the outline of a polygon that turns once per cycle, instead of a circle.
Controls.pwCountTip: How many pendulums swing side by side. More pendulums make finer waves and richer chords; the notes climb a major scale from the slowest one.
Controls.pwBaseOscillationsTip: Swings the slowest pendulum completes per cycle (the classic Harvard wave uses 51). Every next pendulum completes one more, which is what tunes the row to realign exactly once per cycle. Lower numbers give a slow, sparse wave; higher ones a fast, dense one.
Controls.pwCycleSecondsTip: Seconds until the row is back in line. The run ends after the chosen number of cycles.
Controls.pwAmplitudeTip: Swing amplitude in degrees. Wider swings shorten the row's strings so the outermost bobs still fit; the radial and sliding layouts travel further. Bouncing balls ignore it – their heights follow the periods.
Controls.pwPhasingTip: Off: the classic tuning, every pendulum in line again at the end of each cycle. On: the swing times form an arithmetic series (each pendulum's swing lasts a fixed bit longer than the next one's) – a Reich-style tempo phase shift that keeps drifting instead of snapping back.
Controls.pwTrailsTip: How long the fading trails of the bobs last; the spiral arms of the Galaxy layout live in them.
Controls.pwSoundOnTip: When a pendulum sounds: crossing the centre line (twice per swing), reaching an extreme, or both. Bouncing balls play on the floor hit and at the apex.
Controls.pwPitchDirectionTip: Low to high: the slowest (longest) pendulum plays the lowest note. High to low: the other way round. The notes are degrees of a major scale from C4 and are snapped to the scale chosen in the Sound section.
Controls.pwWaveChordTip: Bobs that align within 20 ms play together as one chord – one sound on the beat grid, the level shared out – instead of a pile of separate notes. A chord of most of the row is accented with a flash.
Controls.pwCyclesTip: Full cycles after which the run finishes, with the whole row back in line. 0 keeps it swinging forever.
Controls.finderDesc: Find a simulation seed that runs for the exact duration you select, keeping all your custom settings in mind.
Controls.topTextTip: Custom text overlay displayed above the physics arena.
Controls.bottomTextTip: Custom text overlay displayed below the physics arena.
Controls.textSizeTip: Adjust the font size of the text overlays.
Controls.findSimulationTip: Search for a simulation seed that produces a run of the exact target duration.
Controls.fixedRunLength: Always {duration}s with these settings – change the cycle length or the cycles
Controls.characterTip: Give the ball a personality: a face that looks where it flies, blinks and reacts to hits, breaking walls and escapes, plus a name under it. Purely visual – seeds and found simulations are not affected.
Controls.ballFaceTip: A vector face drawn on the ball (and in the recording). The eyes follow the flight, blink on a seeded schedule, squint on hard hits, go wide when a wall breaks, grin at the escape and close happily at rest.
Controls.ballNameTip: A small name label drawn under the (first) ball, e.g. Boris.
Controls.nameLabelTip: Show the name under the ball, with a subtle outline so it reads on any background.
Controls.ballSquashTip: The ball squashes against whatever it hits and springs back into shape. Visual only – the physics does not change.
Controls.faceOverImageTip: Draw the face over a custom ball image or emoji as well (off keeps the picture's own face).
Controls.faceSoundsTip: The cat face chirps a synthesised meow when it gets hit, when a wall breaks and when it escapes – on the beat grid and in the recording. Not used while the bounce sound is an audio sample.
Controls.faceSoundsSampleNote: Silent while the bounce sound is an audio sample – switch back to tones to hear the cat.
Controls.borisPersonaDesc: Boris always escapes – freedom lasts about 4 seconds. One click sets his face, name and squash.
Controls.themeTip: One-click looks: a theme sets the wall, ball, line, background and trail colours and the particle style. Every colour stays editable afterwards – click the theme again to restore it.
Controls.themeEdited: edited – click it again to restore
Controls.themeBackgroundTip: A solid colour, a top-to-bottom gradient or your own picture behind the arena. The reactive background still flashes on top, and exports continue it into the letterbox bars.
Controls.themeBgError: This picture could not be loaded. Try a PNG, JPG, WebP or GIF file.
Controls.themeBgImageNote: The picture is cover-fitted behind the arena. It stays in your browser and is not part of shared links or presets.
Controls.themeBgDimTip: Darkens the background picture so the balls and walls stand out.
Controls.themeParticlesTip: What bursts out when a wall breaks or a run finishes. With a theme picked, the particles take its colours.
Controls.themeTrailTip: The colour trail flows between two colours of your choice instead of the rainbow.
Controls.prDesc: Voices ticking at their own tempos: every tick plays a note, and whenever all of them tick together the screen flashes and a chord sounds. Positions are exact functions of time, so even 400 voices replay identically.
Controls.prLayoutTip: Rings: a dot on each ring orbits a whole number of times per cycle and ticks at 12 o'clock. Arcs: dots slide back and forth across a circle and tick at both ends. Metronomes: a grid of pendulums ticking at both extremes – pair it with the BPM steps for a tempo phase shift. Spiral: orbiting dots whose tick points lie on a spiral, redrawn at every alignment. You can switch the layout mid-run; the rhythm carries on.
Controls.prArcStyleTip: Chords: every dot slides along its own horizontal chord of a big circle (the "metronomes inside a circle" look). Semicircles: every dot swings along a half circle and ticks on the baseline.
Controls.prPolygonTip: Draws every ring as a polygon with as many corners as its ratio (3 ticks per cycle = a triangle), turning once per cycle so a corner meets the dot at every tick.
Controls.prTemposTip: Harmonic: voice n ticks n times per cycle (1:2:3…), all in phase at the end of every cycle. BPM steps: the tempos climb from a base BPM by a fixed step, so neighbours drift apart slowly and line up again only after a long time. Custom: your own list of ratios such as 3,4,5,7.
Controls.prCountTip: How many voices tick at once, up to 400. More voices make denser patterns; the notes climb a major scale from the slowest one.
Controls.prCycleSecondsTip: Seconds per cycle for the harmonic and custom tempos: a voice with ratio n ticks n times per cycle, and every voice is in phase again at the end of each cycle.
Controls.prBaseBpmTip: Tempo of the first voice, in beats per minute.
Controls.prBpmStepTip: How much faster each next voice ticks, in BPM. Small steps give a slow Reich-style phase shift; the voices line up again once every tempo fits a whole number of ticks into the same time.
Controls.prCustomTip: Whole numbers separated by commas, spaces or colons – each one is a voice ticking that many times per cycle (3:4:5 is the classic polyrhythm). Up to 400 voices.
Controls.prAccentEveryTip: Makes every k-th tick of each voice louder and longer, with a ring around the dot – like the first beat of a bar. 0 turns accents off.
Controls.prPitchByTip: By voice: each voice plays the next degree of a major scale from C4. By ratio: each voice plays its tempo ratio as a harmonic of C3, so 3:4:5 sounds like the chord G–C–E. Both are snapped to the scale chosen in the Sound section.
Controls.prNumbersTip: Writes each voice's ratio (or BPM) on its dot.
Controls.prCyclesTip: Cycles after which the run ends, with every voice back in phase. 0 keeps it ticking forever.
Controls.cpDesc: Hundreds of orbs of different sizes bounce off the walls and off each other – mass follows size – and every collision plays a soft note pitched by the smaller orb: big orbs low, small orbs high.
Controls.cpCountTip: How many orbs collide, from 10 to 2000. They are sized automatically to fill the container (Ball Size makes them bigger or smaller); the ring holds at most 36 lollipops.
Controls.cpSizeSpreadTip: How different the orbs are: 0 makes them all the same size, 100% spreads them from a third to three times the base size. Mass follows the area, so big orbs shove small ones around – and bigger orbs play lower notes.
Controls.cpContainerTip: The shape the orbs bounce around in: a circle or a square, both filling the centre of the video.
Controls.cpGravityTip: How much of the Gravity setting pulls the orbs down. 0 is a floating gas of orbs; higher values heap them up at the bottom while they keep bouncing.
Controls.cpRestitutionTip: Coefficient of restitution of every collision: 1 is perfectly elastic (the orbs never lose energy), 0.7 is soft and damped, so under gravity the orbs settle into a pile.
Controls.cpSquishyTip: Squash and stretch: every impact flattens an orb along the direction of the hit for a split second (120 ms), like a jelly ball. Purely visual.
Controls.cpSyncStartTip: All orbs start on a grid at the same instant – from rest under gravity, or all flying the same way without it – so they fall and bounce in sync. Pair it with Squishy and a Size Variety of 0 for the “squishy balls bounce in sync” clip.
Controls.cpAntiCollisionAtTip: Second of the run at which the collision system switches off: the orbs change colour and pass straight through each other (they still bounce off the container). Off keeps them colliding forever.
Controls.cpRingTip: Constrains the bodies to a circular track: each one is a lollipop – a stick from the centre to a disc – that collides with its neighbours along the ring. With gravity they swing like pendulums around the bottom.
Controls.ballCountTip: How many balls start in the arena, flying out in evenly spread directions (Classic, Multiply, Lines, Shatter and Color Match, up to six; Grow, whose balls grow to fill the ring, up to two; Multiply multiplies them from there). Two is the old two-ball setup; with teams, every ball is a team.
Controls.teamsTip: Give every ball a team: a name, a colour and an emoji. The canvas labels the balls, keeps score per team (bounces, walls broken, escapes) and crowns a winner when the run ends – in the recording too. Winner: most escapes, then most walls broken, then most bounces.
Controls.teamsModeNote: Teams play in the modes with several balls: Classic, Multiply, Lines, Shatter, Color Match and Grow.
Controls.teamsModeCapNote: This mode plays with at most {max} balls: the first {max} teams play, the others wait for another mode.
Controls.showBallNamesTip: Show each team's name above its ball.
Controls.showScoreboardTip: Bounces, walls broken and escapes of every team in a corner of the video, the leader on top.
Controls.scoreboardPositionTip: The corner of the exported square the scoreboard sits in.
Controls.cameraGroupTip: Cinematic camera effects. They only change the picture and the pace at which the clock feeds the simulation, never the physics: seeds and found simulations play out exactly the same.
Controls.cameraGroupDesc: Zoom in on the ball, shake the view when a wall breaks, slow down on near misses and replay the escape – in the preview and in recordings.
Controls.cameraZoomTip: How far the view zooms toward the ball, following it around the arena. 0 keeps today's view (with Camera Follow on, the gentle classic follow). With several balls (Ball Count) the zoom stays wide enough to keep them all in frame.
Controls.screenShakeTip: Shakes the view every time a wall breaks; the shake dies out over 300 ms. Higher values shake harder.
Controls.slowMoOnNearMissTip: When the ball squeezes through a gap right next to its edge (the Drama Director's near miss), time slows down for a moment. The simulation runs the same steps, just slower – recordings show the slow motion.
Controls.slowMoFactorTip: How fast time runs during the slow motion: 0.2× is very slow, 0.8× barely slower.
Controls.slowMoMsTip: How long each slow-motion moment lasts, in real time. Afterwards a short pause keeps back-to-back near misses from slowing down the whole run.
Controls.replayOnEscapeTip: When a ball escapes the outer wall and the run ends, its last 2 seconds play again at half speed with a REPLAY badge before the end screen – in recordings too.
Controls.replayOnEscapeModes: The replay plays in the escape modes: Classic, Accumulation, Portal, Shatter and Color Match.
Controls.glassDesc: Stages of glass panes stand between the ball and HOME. Every landing cracks a pane and plays the next note (the next melody note, or a scale degree by row); the last hit shatters it with the wall-break sound – a glass clip unless you pick another. Each new stage brings more panes, thicker ones, sliding ones and ones with holes.
Controls.glassRowsTip: How many glass panes the first stage holds, from 3 to 30. Every later stage adds a third more (up to 30), packed closer together, so the hits speed up as the ball gets deeper.
Controls.glassHpTip: How many landings a pane of the first stage takes before it shatters, from 1 to 5; every hit grows another crack from the impact point. Every other stage the glass gets one hit thicker (at most two more).
Controls.glassStagesTip: How many stages the ball smashes through before it reaches HOME, from 1 to 10. The camera scrolls down to each new stage and a banner announces it.
Controls.glassMovingTip: From the third stage on, some panes are narrower and slide left and right: the ball can miss one and drop past it – a lucky escape – or bounce up into it from below.
Controls.glassHolesTip: From the second stage on, some panes have a hole the ball must miss to keep smashing. Dropping through it skips that pane (the ball can still crack it from below).
Controls.glassRunSize: Whole run: {panes} panes and up to {hits} hits over {stages} stage(s), then HOME.
Controls.mpDesc: Speed, size, damage, bounce and gravity multipliers stack on the ball – with no cap unless you set one. Pickups float in the ring modes, and a ball whose damage reaches the smash level breaks the rings it touches.
Controls.multiplierPickupsTip: Floating orbs – x2 SPEED, x1.5 SIZE, x2 DMG, x2 BALLS… – appear at seeded times and places inside the ball's ring. Touching one stacks it on the ball with a burst, a rising arpeggio and a pop of the HUD badge. Seeds and Find Simulation include them.
Controls.pickupRateTip: How many orbs appear per 10 seconds on average (0–3).
Controls.pickupTypesTip: Which orbs may appear. x2 BALLS clones the ball (up to the Ball Cap of the ball interaction) and only floats in the modes that play with several balls.
Controls.pickupBallsUnavailable: x2 BALLS only floats in Classic, Multiply, Lines, Shatter and Grow.
Controls.pickupLifetimeTip: Seconds an orb drifts before it fades away.
Controls.mpUnlimitedTip: On (default): multipliers stack without any cap – the speed can keep doubling. The physics stays safe at any value: more sub-steps per frame, and past 64 the clock slows down (SLOW-MO) instead of letting a ball tunnel through a wall.
Controls.mpCapTip: With Unlimited off: the highest value any stat may stack to (and 1/cap the lowest). 0 = no cap.
Controls.wallSmashThresholdTip: Once a ball's damage multiplier reaches this value it smashes the rings it touches – no gap needed – with the wall-break effect and sound (Classic, Accumulation, Multiply, Shatter, Color Match, Portal).
Controls.mpBoardDesc: Balls fall through rows of gates to HOME: count gates clone them, speed, size and damage gates stack multipliers, ÷2 takes half away and release doors let them through in bursts.
Controls.mpRowsTip: Rows of gates between the start and HOME, 4 to 20. The camera scrolls down with the lowest ball.
Controls.mpStartBallsTip: Balls released at the top, 1 to 10.
Controls.mpMaxBallsTip: Most balls in play at once (50–2000): count gates stop cloning there. Balls that reach HOME free their place.
Controls.mpGateMixTip: How often each kind of gate appears (0 = never, 9 = most often). The layout itself is drawn from the seed.
Controls.mpTargetTip: Rigging: with a target, Find Simulation searches for a seed whose final HOME count is within 5 % of it (instead of a duration). 0 = off.
Controls.captionsDesc: Animated overlays for the clip: a countdown, a wall counter, a progress bar, a question that reveals its answer, or your own text. They are drawn on the canvas, so every recording includes them.
Controls.captionsTip: Each caption enters and leaves with a fade, slide or pop animation between its start and end time. The timing runs on the simulation clock: pausing holds the captions, 8× plays them eight times faster and Restart starts them over. Captions travel in the share link and are saved in presets.
Controls.captionsEmpty: No captions yet – add one below.
Controls.captionAddTip: Adds a caption of that type (up to {max}). Captions at the same position stack in the order of the list.
Controls.captionsClipNote: The countdown and the progress bar run to the clip length set in Recording ({duration}s).
Controls.captionTypeTip: Countdown: the time left to the end of the clip. Wall counter: walls broken out of the walls in play ("Wall 3/10"; hidden in the modes without rings). Progress bar: the elapsed time over the clip length. Question: a question whose answer pops in when a ball escapes or the run finishes. Text: any text.
Controls.captionTextTip: The text to show (up to 80 characters; a long text wraps onto up to three lines).
Controls.captionQuestionTip: The question to show, e.g. "Will it escape?" – an empty field shows that one.
Controls.captionCountdownLabelTip: Optional text around the time: [time] is replaced by the time left ("[time] left"); a label without it goes in front of the time.
Controls.captionWallLabelTip: Optional text instead of "Wall [n]/[total]": [n] is the walls broken and [total] the walls in play; a label without them goes in front of the count.
Controls.captionProgressLabelTip: Optional text above the bar; [pct] is replaced by the elapsed percentage.
Controls.captionAnswerTip: Revealed under the question the moment a ball escapes or the run finishes – it pops in and stays until the end. Leave it empty to show the question only.
Controls.captionPositionTip: Top, center or bottom of the exported square. Captions at the same position stack; the top ones keep clear of the scoreboard.
Controls.captionStartTip: Second of the run (simulation time) at which the caption enters.
Controls.captionEndTip: Second at which the caption has left. 0 – or any time not after the start – keeps it until the end of the run.
Controls.captionAnimationTip: How the caption enters and leaves: fades in and out, slides in from its edge of the frame, or pops in with a bounce.
Controls.captionSizeTip: Text size, 0.5× to 3×; the progress bar gets thicker too.
Controls.captionBackgroundTip: A rounded box behind the text (the track of the progress bar). Off: the text gets a soft shadow instead.

classic.name: Classic
classic.description: A ball bounces inside concentric rings that each have a single gap. Every wall it slips through breaks with a satisfying effect. Simple, hypnotic and endlessly rewatchable.

accumulation.name: Accumulation
accumulation.description: The ball has a few seconds to escape before it freezes where it is. Every frozen ball becomes an obstacle for the next one. Will the last ball make it out?

multiply.name: Multiply
multiply.description: Each time a ball escapes the ring it spawns extra balls. The arena fills with bouncing chaos within seconds, which makes for explosive, shareable clips.

lines.name: Lines
lines.description: Every bounce point is connected to the ball by a line, so the run slowly draws intricate string art as the ball ricochets around the circle.

paint.name: Paint
paint.description: The ball paints a rainbow trail wherever it goes, gradually colouring the whole circle while a live percentage counter tracks the coverage.

target.name: Target
target.description: Numbered segments line the wall and must be hit in order. Every correct hit triggers a wall-break effect; wrong hits flash red.

grow.name: Grow
grow.description: The ball is sealed inside one large ring and grows a little with every bounce, filling more and more of the space until there is nowhere left to go.

shatter.name: Shatter
shatter.description: Every wall is made of segments with hit points. Each bounce cracks a segment and enough hits shatter it. Clear a path through every wall to escape.

colorMatch.name: Color Match
colorMatch.description: The wall is split into coloured segments and the ball changes colour on every bounce. A segment only breaks when the colours match. Clear them all to escape.

portal.name: Portal
portal.description: Colour-matched portal pairs sit on the wall. Touch one and the ball teleports to its twin. After enough uses the portals burn out and become exits.

drop.name: Ball Drop
drop.description: Balls of different sizes and weights rain down through rows of pegs and bars, and every hit plays a note pitched by the ball's size. Different gravities fall out of step and the run writes its own polyrhythm.

box.name: Bouncing Shapes
box.description: Squares, circles or DVD-style logos glide through a box at constant speed and every wall hit plays the next note. Big numbers count down with each bounce, logos at speeds in 2:3 or 3:4:5 ratios weave polyrhythms, and a corner hit is the accent everyone waits for.

pendulum.name: Pendulum Wave
pendulum.description: Pendulums tuned so each one swings once more per cycle than the last: the row drifts into travelling waves, splits into groups and snaps back in line every cycle, every crossing a note. Row, arc, circle, galaxy, sliding or bouncing – and a phasing mode that never quite realigns.

polyrhythm.name: Metronomes & Polyrhythms
polyrhythm.description: Up to 400 voices tick at their own tempos – dots orbiting rings in 3:4:5, dots sliding across a circle, a grid of metronomes phasing apart, a spiral – and every tick is a note. They drift into polyrhythms and snap back in phase with a flash and a chord.

collide.name: Collision Playground
collide.description: Hundreds of varied orbs collide in a circle or a box and every collision plays a soft note pitched by size. Make them squishy, drop them in sync, switch the collisions off mid-run or put lollipops on a ring.

glass.name: Glass Smash
glass.description: Boris is determined to smash all of the glass: he drops down a shaft of glass panes, every landing cracks the pane under him and plays a note, and the last hit shatters it. Stage after stage the glass gets denser and thicker, starts to slide and grows holes – until he rolls through the door marked HOME.

multipliers.name: Multipliers
multipliers.description: Boris uses the multipliers to get home: balls fall through rows of gates – x2, x3 and x5 clone them, x2 SPEED, x1.5 SIZE and x2 DMG stack with no cap, ÷2 takes half away and release doors let them through in bursts – past bumpers and blockers, while a live counter shows how many make it home.

wallBreak.name: Wall Break Effects
wallBreak.description: Confetti, glass shatter, a shockwave, all three at once, or none. Every time the ball breaks through a wall, your chosen effect plays.

rainbowWalls.name: Rainbow Walls
rainbowWalls.description: Walls cycle through the spectrum in two styles: a smooth gradient across all rings, or a reactive pulse that flashes colour on every hit.

glow.name: Ball & Wall Glow
glow.description: Toggle a soft radial glow around the ball and a flash on the walls independently, so you get exactly the amount of shine you want.

colorTrail.name: Colour Trail
colorTrail.description: The ball leaves a vivid, hue-shifting streak behind it, so fast motion reads as intentional rather than messy.

reactiveBg.name: Reactive Background
reactiveBg.description: The backdrop pulses and shifts colour with every bounce, making each hit feel heavier.

bouncier.name: Increasing Bounciness
bouncier.description: The ball speeds up with every wall hit until it finally breaks free, then the boost resets for the next ring.

customBall.name: Custom Ball Image
customBall.description: Replace the ball with your own image or an emoji: a logo, a face, a product. It scales and moves with the ball.

textOverlays.name: Text Overlays
textOverlays.description: Add a top and a bottom caption with adjustable size for hooks, branding or calls to action, baked into the export.

spikes.name: Spikes
spikes.description: Add inward-pointing spikes to the outer wall that freeze the ball on contact, raising the stakes in Accumulation mode.

videoExport.name: Video Export
videoExport.description: Record the run as an MP4 in square, HD, Full HD or vertical TikTok (1080×1920) format, from 10 to 120 seconds long.

savePresets.name: Save & Load Presets
savePresets.description: Store the whole configuration, mode, colours, physics and effects, in your browser and load it back with one click.

watermark.name: Custom Watermark
watermark.description: Stamp your handle faintly in the centre of the ring so reposts still credit you.

customSound.name: Custom Sound
customSound.description: Pick a melody from the built-in library or import your own MIDI file, and every wall hit plays the next note. Play an audio clip – built-in or uploaded – on every bounce instead, or upload a whole song and let each bounce play its next slice. Choose one of seven instruments, snap every bounce to a musical scale and lock the sounds to a BPM grid.

q1.question: Is {siteName} free to use?
q1.answer: Yes. The simulator, every mode, every customisation option and the video export are free, and there is no account to create.

q2.question: What video formats and resolutions can I export?
q2.answer: You can record 500×500 (square), 1280×720 (HD), 1920×1080 (Full HD) and 1080×1920 (vertical, TikTok) clips between 10 and 120 seconds long. Browsers that support MP4 recording export MP4; others export WebM.

q3.question: Can I use the exported videos commercially?
q3.answer: Yes. Everything you create is yours to use on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram or anywhere else, with no attribution required.

q4.question: Do I need to install anything?
q4.answer: No. The whole tool runs in your browser. Open the site and start creating.

q5.question: Can I save my settings?
q5.answer: Yes. Save as many presets as you like to your browser's local storage and load them back at any time. The URL also updates as you tweak settings, so you can bookmark or share a setup.

q6.question: Does it work on mobile?
q6.answer: The simulator is designed for desktop browsers, where there is room for the canvas and the controls side by side. It runs on phones too, but a laptop or desktop is the better experience.

q7.question: Are there keyboard shortcuts?
q7.answer: Yes. Press Space to pause or resume and R to restart the simulation.

q8.question: How do I upload a custom ball image?
q8.answer: Open the Ball & Physics section, enable Show Advanced Options and click Choose Image. Any image works: logos, photos, memes. Or pick an emoji from the emoji grid.

q9.question: How does the custom sound feature work?
q9.answer: In the Custom Sound section, choose a song from the built-in library or import a MIDI file. The melody is extracted from the file and every wall hit plays its next note, turning the run into a musical performance. Prefer a sound effect? Switch Bounce Sound to Audio sample and pick a built-in click, pluck or kick, or upload your own clip – it is pitched per wall and included in the recording.

q10.question: What makes {siteName} a satisfying ball simulator?
q10.answer: The loop is simple: a ball bounces inside rings with tiny gaps, and every time it slips through something rewarding happens: confetti, a shatter, a shockwave. Because you control physics, colours and effects, the tension and the payoff look exactly the way you want.

q11.question: Can I use {siteName} as a satisfying ball clicker?
q11.answer: It is not a clicker game, but it scratches the same itch. You watch, anticipate the gap and get rewarded with effects and sound on every escape. The run plays itself, so it is the satisfaction without the tapping.

AboutTool.title: What {siteName} actually is
AboutTool.p1: {siteName} is a browser tool for making the bouncing-ball videos that fill TikTok, Reels and YouTube Shorts. Pick a mode, adjust a few settings, press record and download the clip. There is no account, no installation and no video editor involved; everything happens in the tab you already have open, so an idea becomes a finished video in a couple of minutes.
AboutTool.p2: The format works because it is simple. A ball bounces inside a ring with a gap. Every time it slips through, something pays off: a wall shatters, the ball multiplies, colour floods the screen, a target is hit. Viewers want to know how it ends, so they keep watching. That small loop of tension and release is what drives the views, and here you control every part of it instead of reposting someone else's clip.
AboutTool.p3: Each of the eleven modes tells a different kind of story. Classic is the one most people picture: a ball breaking out through rings. Multiply turns one ball into a swarm. Accumulation freezes balls in place until the last one has to thread a maze of its predecessors. Paint, Target, Grow, Shatter, Color Match, Lines, Portal and Ball Drop each change the rules in their own way. Switching takes one click and the canvas updates immediately.
AboutTool.p4: The look is yours. Add rings for a longer build-up or remove them for a fast payoff. Turn on rainbow walls, switch the break effect between confetti, shatter and shockwave, or stack all three. Add spikes for danger, glow for polish and a colour trail so fast motion looks deliberate. Put your own image on the ball, write a hook like "will it escape?" across the top and load a melody so the bounces land on a beat. Small changes matter: one extra ring can be the difference between a clip people skip and one they watch twice.
AboutTool.p5: When the run looks right, record it in the browser and export a video sized for vertical feeds. No screen-capture app, no unwanted watermark, no re-encoding elsewhere. Found a combination you like? Save it as a preset and reuse it for a whole series; many accounts post the same mode every day with small variations.
AboutTool.p6: Reposting a clip that a hundred other accounts already used gives the algorithm, and your audience, nothing new. When you build the run yourself you decide the hook, the colours, the pacing and the moment it pays off. You can match a trending sound, add your handle and post a fresh version every day without repeating yourself, and original content never trips the reused-content filters that quietly limit reach.
AboutTool.p7: The defaults already produce a clip worth posting. From there, change one thing at a time and watch what happens: add a ring, swap the break effect, turn the glow up. Because the canvas reacts immediately you learn what each setting does by using it, and after a few sessions you develop a feel for which combinations land.
AboutTool.p8: Most people here are creators chasing reach without a budget: no camera, no studio, no design background, just a hook and a few minutes of tuning. Teachers use it to show motion and collisions in a way students actually watch. Plenty of people open it just to play, because a ball smashing through rings is fun on its own. The controls are the same for everyone.
AboutTool.p9_before: {siteName} is free. Presets and settings live in your own browser, videos render on your own machine and there is no sign-up wall. If you want to go deeper on a mode or find settings that tend to perform, the
AboutTool.p9_mid: breaks each one down with examples, and if something feels off or you wish a setting existed, the
AboutTool.p9_after: goes straight to the person building it.

Instructions.title: Every control, explained
Instructions.description: This is the simulator layout: a live canvas on the left and the controls panel on the right. The numbers on the mockup match the steps beside it.
Instructions.mockupCaption: A simplified view of the simulator screen.

step1.title: Pick a mode
step1.body: Open the Mode row in the controls panel and choose one of the eleven modes. The mode sets the rules, so decide it first.

step2.title: Open a section and tweak it
step2.body: Ball, Wall, Visual and Sound each expand when clicked. Change the wall count, the break effect, the colours or the trail. In a hurry? Type a setting name into the search box at the top.

step3.title: Press Start
step3.body: Hit Start simulator on the canvas. The defaults already look good, so start right away and adjust once you see it move.

step4.title: Get the run right
step4.body: While it plays, use Restart to reroll, Pause to hold a frame and the speed buttons (1x to 8x) to skip ahead. Space pauses, R restarts. Reset until the timing lands the way you want.

step5.title: Set length and size
step5.body: Open the Recording section to choose how long the clip runs and its resolution. 1080×1920 is the vertical size for TikTok, Reels and Shorts.

step6.title: Record, and it downloads
step6.body: Press Record video. It captures the run with sound and saves the file to your device. Like the setup? Save it as a preset and reuse it for a whole series.

mode.what: The core game. Sets the goal and the rules.

ballPhysics.name: Ball physics
ballPhysics.what: Speed, size, gravity, colour and bounce.

wallsGap.name: Walls / Gap
wallsGap.what: How many rings and how wide the opening is.

wallBreakEffect.name: Wall break effect
wallBreakEffect.what: Confetti, shatter, shockwave, all or none.

visualEffects.name: Visual effects
visualEffects.what: Rainbow walls, glow and the colour trail.

reactiveBackground.name: Reactive background
reactiveBackground.what: Pulses the backdrop in time with hits.

spikes.name: Spikes

customBall.name: Custom ball
customBall.what: Puts your own image or an emoji on the ball.

textOverlay.name: Text overlay

customSound.name: Custom sound

watermark.name: Watermark

speed.name: Speed (1x to 8x)
speed.what: Fast-forwards a long run while you preview.

savePreset.what: Stores the whole setup to load again in one click.

Editorial.physicsP1: Every run starts from the same idea: a ball bouncing inside a ring. Speed, gravity and bounciness change how it moves, a bit like dropping a real ball into a bowl and deciding how fast it falls and how hard it ricochets. The engine steps the world sixty times per second with several sub-steps per frame, so collisions stay stable even at high speed.
Editorial.physicsP2: Each ring has a small gap. When the ball lines up with it and passes through, the ring breaks with the effect you picked: confetti, shattering glass or a shockwave. The ball moves on to the next ring, and the process repeats until it escapes or the recording ends.
Editorial.physicsP3: Every mode layers its own rules on top: the ball might split into a swarm, freeze into an obstacle course, or grow with every bounce. All of it runs locally in your browser; nothing is uploaded and the video is encoded on your own machine.
Editorial.modeClassic: A single ball bounces through concentric rings, each with a gap. Break through every wall to escape. The default mode: simple, hypnotic and endlessly watchable.
Editorial.modeAccumulation: The ball has limited time to escape. If it fails, it freezes in place and becomes a new obstacle, and a fresh ball spawns. The arena fills up fast. Can the last one get out?
Editorial.modeMultiply: Each time a ball escapes the ring it spawns extra balls, so one ball quickly becomes a swarm. Great for explosive, chaotic clips that fill the screen.
Editorial.modeLines: Every bounce point is connected to the ball by a line, producing intricate geometric patterns. Part physics, part generative art.
Editorial.modePaint: The ball leaves a colourful trail as it moves, gradually covering the circle. A percentage counter tracks how much you have painted. Try to reach 100%.
Editorial.modeTarget: Numbered segments appear on the wall. Hit them in order; each correct hit triggers a break effect, and wrong hits flash red.
Editorial.modePortal: Colour-matched portal pairs sit on the wall. Touch one to teleport to its twin. After enough uses the portals burn out and the ball breaks free.
Editorial.modeShatter: Walls are split into segments with hit points. Each bounce cracks a segment and after enough hits it shatters. Clear a path through all walls to escape.
Editorial.modeColorMatch: The wall is split into coloured segments and the ball changes colour on every bounce. A segment breaks only when the colours match. Clear them all to win.
Editorial.modeGrow: The ball is sealed inside a single ring and grows with every bounce, taking up more and more of the space until it can barely move.
Editorial.modeDrop: A tall board of pegs and bars instead of rings. Balls of different sizes and weights drop from the top and every hit plays a note, big balls low and small balls high, until they all come to rest – or forever with Rain on.
Editorial.modeBox: A rectangular box instead of rings. Squares, circles or DVD-style logos travel in straight lines at constant speed and reflect perfectly off the walls; every hit plays the next note of the melody or a note that depends on the wall. Each shape carries a big number that counts down per bounce, flashes, grows a little and changes colour, and several logos at speeds in ratios like 2:3 or 3:4:5 weave a polyrhythm until every number reaches zero – or forever with the countdown off. A logo that hits a corner plays a louder note and lights up the screen.
Editorial.modePendulum: No rings: 5–60 pendulums tuned like the classic pendulum wave, so the slowest swings K times per cycle and every next one once more. In line at the start, they drift into travelling waves, split into two and three groups and snap back in line at the end of every cycle; a centre crossing (or an extreme) plays a note pitched by the pendulum's place in the row, and bobs that align play one chord. Six layouts – a row under a bar, an arc of pivots swinging toward the centre, bobs on radii from the centre or on a rotating polygon, a slowly turning galaxy that draws spiral arms, sliders on rails and balls bouncing on a floor – plus a phasing option that turns the tuning into a Reich-style tempo phase shift.
Editorial.tipFindSimulationBody: Rather than guessing, let the tool search for a seed that produces a run of your target length. Open Find Simulation below the canvas, set the duration and let it scan seeds. Once it finds one, the run lasts exactly that long, which makes recording predictable.
Editorial.tipLayerEffectsBody: Rainbow walls, glow, colour trails and wall-break effects stack. Try a reactive background with confetti breaks and a glow; the extra layers keep viewers watching.
Editorial.tipTextHooksBody: Top and bottom overlays give context. A question like "Will it escape?" or a countdown builds anticipation. Adjust the text size so it is readable at a glance on a phone.
Editorial.tipClipLengthTitle: Match the clip length to the platform
Editorial.tipClipLengthBody: Shorter clips (15 to 30 seconds) tend to perform better on TikTok and Reels. Set the duration in the Recording section and pick the vertical 1080×1920 resolution.
Editorial.tipPresetsTitle: Save your favourite setups as presets
Editorial.tipPresetsBody: When a configuration works, save it and load it again for your next video. Consistent series perform well because the audience knows what to expect.
Editorial.tipSpeedBody: Use the 2× to 8× speed buttons to fast-forward through a long run while previewing. Before recording, set it back to 1× so the export captures every frame at full quality.
Editorial.troubleExportQ: The video export looks wrong or is missing frames
Editorial.troubleExportA: Use a recent version of Chrome, Edge or Firefox; recording works best there. Close other tabs and apps to free up memory, and keep the simulator tab visible while it records. Chrome and Safari export MP4; Firefox exports WebM, which every major platform accepts.
Editorial.troubleAudioQ: The simulation does not play audio
Editorial.troubleAudioA: Browsers block sound until you interact with the page. Click anywhere first, then press Start. If there is still no sound, check the system volume and make sure the site is allowed to play audio.
Editorial.troubleSpeedQ: The ball moves too fast or too slow
Editorial.troubleSpeedA: Open the Ball & Physics section and adjust Ball Speed. Lower values are easier to follow; higher values give more energetic clips. Gravity also changes the pacing: lower gravity keeps the ball floating longer between hits.
Editorial.troubleSettingsA: Presets are stored in your browser's local storage. Clearing site data or using a private window removes them. Copy the share link of a setup you care about so you can restore it later.
Editorial.troubleMidiQ: My custom MIDI file does not load
Editorial.troubleMidiA: Very complex files with many simultaneous tracks may not parse. Try a simpler single-melody MIDI (format 0 or 1). The tool keeps only the highest note at each moment, so a lead-melody export from your music software works best.
Editorial.troubleStuckA: Send a note through the feedback page and describe what you were doing.
Editorial.modePolyrhythm: No rings to escape: 2–400 voices each tick at their own tempo and every tick plays a note. Rings (dots orbiting 1, 2, 3… times per cycle and ticking at 12 o'clock, optionally as rotating polygons), arcs (dots sliding along the chords or semicircles of a circle and ticking at both ends), a grid of metronomes, or a spiral whose tick points line up again every cycle. The tempos follow the harmonic series, an arithmetic BPM series (the Reich-style tempo phase shift) or your own ratio list such as 3,4,5,7. The moment every voice ticks together is computed exactly and lands as a chord and a flash; the run ends after the chosen number of cycles and always lasts the same time, so it fits any clip.
Editorial.modeCollide: No rings: 10 to 2000 orbs of different sizes – mass follows size – bounce around a circle or a square and off each other with elastic collisions, under as much or as little gravity as you like. Every collision plays a soft note pitched by the smaller orb (big orbs low, small orbs high, on a pentatonic ladder snapped to your scale), and only the dozen most energetic collisions of each frame sound, so hundreds of orbs sound like rain on glass instead of noise. Variants: squishy orbs that squash on every impact, a sync start that drops them all from a grid at once, an anti-collision switch that lets them pass through each other at a chosen second, and lollipops on a ring that collide along a circular track.
Editorial.modeGlass: The borisbounces glass format, no rings: a portrait shaft of horizontal glass panes stands between the ball and a doorway marked HOME. The ball falls and every landing cracks the pane below it – a procedural crack grows from the impact point – and plays the next note of your melody or, without one, a scale degree by row; on its last hit a pane shatters into shards with an accented note and a glass-break sound, and the ball crashes through to the next pane. After the last pane of a stage the camera scrolls down to the next one: more panes, thicker glass, panes that slide left and right and panes with holes the ball must miss. The final stage ends with the ball rolling into the doorway and a celebration. Every run is deterministic, so Find Simulation can pick a seed for your clip length.
Editorial.modeMultipliers: A tall board the camera scrolls down, always following the lowest ball. Every row is split into 2–4 gates: count gates (x2, x3, x5) clone each ball that passes – up to a ball cap you choose, from 50 to 2000 –, speed, size and damage gates stack multipliers on it with no upper limit, ÷2 gates absorb every second ball and release gates hold a pile on a door that opens in bursts. Splitter pegs, kicking bumpers, funnels and blockers with hit points (the damage multiplier wears them down faster) sit between the rows, every hit is a note on a pentatonic plinko piano, and the HOME zone at the bottom counts the arrivals live until the final “N Boris made it home”. A ball that grows wider than the board outgrows it and ends the run with a celebration. Set a target count and Find Simulation looks for a seed whose final count lands within 5 % of it. The same multipliers float as pickup orbs in the ring modes (Ball section → Multipliers).

introduction.title: 1. Introduction
introduction.content: Welcome to {siteDomain} ("we", "our", "us"). We respect your privacy and keep the amount of information connected to your use of this site as small as possible. This policy explains what is collected, how it is used and what your rights are.

information.title: 2. Information We Collect
information.subtitle: We collect the minimum needed to run and improve the service:

analytics.label: Analytics data:
analytics.content: If analytics are enabled, we use a privacy-focused service that records anonymous usage statistics such as page views, browser type, screen size and approximate region. It does not identify you personally.

localStorage.label: Local storage data:
localStorage.content: Your simulator settings and presets are stored in your browser's local storage. They never leave your device and are not sent to our servers.

images.label: Uploaded images and audio:
images.content: Custom ball images, MIDI files and sound clips are processed entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded, stored or transmitted.

howWeUse.title: 3. How We Use Your Information
howWeUse.content: Analytics data is used only to understand how the site is used so we can improve it. We do not sell, share or transfer collected data to third parties for marketing.

cookies.title: 4. Cookies and Tracking

TikTokBallVideos.metaTitle: Make Bouncing Ball Videos for TikTok – Free Tool – {siteName}
TikTokBallVideos.metaDescription: Create hypnotic bouncing-ball videos for TikTok with {siteName}: a free browser tool with 12 modes, custom physics and vertical 1080×1920 export. No sign-up needed.
TikTokBallVideos.title: Bouncing Ball Videos for TikTok
TikTokBallVideos.p1: Bouncing-ball simulations are one of the most dependable formats on TikTok. The premise is tiny, a ball trapped inside rings with narrow gaps trying to bounce its way out, but the payoff is satisfying enough to hold attention for a whole short-form clip. {siteName} is a free browser tool built for exactly this kind of content, with physics controls, visual effects and one-click vertical export.
TikTokBallVideos.p2: What makes the format work is its built-in tension arc. The ball ricochets faster, the walls close in, the gap looks impossibly small, and then the ball slips through and everything pays off with confetti, a shatter or a shockwave. That loop fits naturally into 15 to 60 seconds, which is where TikTok engagement peaks.
TikTokBallVideos.p3: TikTok rewards videos that hold viewers to the end and get replayed. Ball physics does both: people stay to see whether the ball escapes and rewatch to catch the effects they missed. The format also fits TikTok's sound culture: {siteName} can play a melody note by note on every wall hit, turning the physics into a musical performance.
TikTokBallVideos.p4: There is no dialogue, no face on screen and no setup. Just a clean visual hook that works even as background noise for a scrolling viewer, which is why the format regularly out-performs more produced content in the discovery feed.
TikTokBallVideos.p5: TikTok's preferred aspect ratio is 9:16 vertical, 1080×1920 pixels. {siteName} records directly at that size, so there is no cropping, no re-encoding and no external editor. Set the recording duration (10 to 120 seconds), press record and download a platform-ready clip.
TikTokBallVideos.p6: You can also export 500×500 (square), 1280×720 (HD) or 1920×1080 (Full HD) for Reels, YouTube Shorts and other platforms. Recording happens entirely in your browser; nothing is uploaded and no watermark is added unless you add your own.
TikTokBallVideos.p7: The best TikTok ball videos follow a simple recipe: a clear visual hook in the first second, a visible progress indicator such as the number of walls left, and a satisfying payoff when the ball finally escapes. The Find Simulation tool searches for a seed that produces a run of your target length, so you can plan the clip instead of guessing.
TikTokBallVideos.p8: All eleven modes, Classic, Accumulation, Multiply, Lines, Paint, Target, Grow, Shatter, Color Match, Portal and Ball Drop, produce a different rhythm, so you can vary your content without starting over. Save your favourite setups as presets and post a new video every day with one click.

About.metaTitle: About {siteName} – Free Ball Physics Video Maker
About.metaDescription: The story behind {siteName}: a free, browser-based tool for making the bouncing-ball videos that go viral on TikTok, Reels and YouTube Shorts.
About.metaOgDescription: Why {siteName} exists and who it is for.
About.title: About {siteName}
About.p1: {siteName} started with a simple frustration. Bouncing-ball physics videos were everywhere, pulling in millions of views, and every way of making one was clunky: learn a game engine, pay for an app, or repost a clip a thousand other accounts had already used. None of that suited someone who just wanted to make a good video and post it. So we built the tool we wished existed: open a tab, make the video, download it, done.
About.p2: That idea still runs the whole site. {siteName} is free, works in your browser and asks nothing of you before you start. No sign-up, no install, no paywall between you and a finished clip. The defaults already produce something worth posting; everything after that is you shaping it to fit your idea.
About.p3: Speed and control, more than anything else. Speed, because the gap between an idea and a posted video is where most content dies; if a clip takes twenty minutes and three apps, you stop making clips. Control, because reposted content does not grow an account. When you set the mode, the colours, the pacing and the hook yourself, the video is yours and it stands a real chance in a feed that has seen every recycled clip.
About.p4: We also care about staying out of your way. The simulator updates as you change things, so you learn by doing rather than reading a manual. Settings have plain names. The hard part, the physics and the rendering, happens quietly in the background while you focus on whether the video is fun to watch.
About.p5: Your work stays with you. Presets and settings live in your browser and videos render on your own machine, not on a server we control. We are not interested in harvesting your data or locking your creations behind an account. The less we know about you, the better the tool feels to use. The details are in our <privacy>privacy policy</privacy>.
About.p6: {siteName} is a small, independent project rather than a venture-backed company with a roadmap full of upsells, and that shapes what gets built. New modes and settings appear because creators ask for them. When you write in through the <feedback>feedback page</feedback>, the note reaches the person actually working on the tool, and a lot of what is in the simulator today exists because someone asked for it.
About.p7: The plan is to keep the core free and keep adding modes, effects and quality-of-life touches that make a good clip faster to build. On the <blog>blog</blog> we break down which settings tend to perform and why certain videos hook people, so the tool and the knowledge around it grow together. If you make something with it, that is the whole point. Go make a ball smash through some walls.
